title: Read the pattern from its end
hook: Must a search look at every letter of the text?

knows: KMP never moves back in the text (kmp-never-steps-back)
doesNotKnow: that comparing the pattern from its end lets you skip text and look at fewer characters than the text has

misconception: Any search must look at every character of the text at least once.
objective: The learner can explain that a mismatch against a text letter that is not in the pattern rules out every placement covering it, so Horspool finds EXAMPLE in a 24-letter text with 15 comparisons in 5 placements and never reads 11 letters, while the plain method reads all 24 with 27 comparisons.

claims.text: Horspool finds EXAMPLE in "HERE IS A SIMPLE EXAMPLE" with 15 character comparisons in 5 placements.
claims.source: Builder's node script (2026-10-14, algo2-sc) and HORS in Demo.tsx: compare right to left; on a miss slide by the table entry of the text letter under the pattern's last position. Placements 0, 7, 9, 15, 17; slide log 0:S->7, 7:P->2, 9:E->6, 15:P->2, 17:match. A comparison is one text letter against one pattern letter. The brief said 4 alignments; the spec corrected it to 5 and this build reproduces 5.

claims.text: The plain left-to-right method takes 27 comparisons over 18 placements and reads all 24 letters.
claims.source: Builder's node script and PLAIN in Demo.tsx: placements 0..17, each reading left to right until a miss or a full match; 27 comparisons; the set of text positions read has 24 members.

claims.text: Horspool never reads 11 of the 24 letters.
claims.source: Builder's node script: the set of text positions Horspool compares has 13 members (position 13 is read twice), so 24 - 13 = 11 are never read.

claims.text: The slide table for EXAMPLE is E 6, X 5, A 4, M 3, P 2, L 1, any other letter 7.
claims.source: Horspool's table: for each letter in the pattern except the last position, the distance from its last occurrence to the end (E at 0 -> 6, X 5, A 4, M 3, P 2, L 1); letters not in P[0..5] get the pattern length 7. Horspool 1980, Software: Practice and Experience 10(6) (from memory, not opened).

claims.text: The first check met S; S is not in EXAMPLE, so no placement covering it could match, and the pattern jumped 7.
claims.source: At placement 0 the pattern's last letter E is under text position 6, which is S. Every placement 1..6 would put some pattern letter over that S, and S is not in EXAMPLE, so none can match; the next possible placement is 7. Node log confirms the first slide is 7.

claims.text: Horspool compares from the pattern's end and, on a miss, slides by the table entry of the text letter under the pattern's end.
claims.source: Horspool 1980, 'Practical fast searching in strings', Software: Practice and Experience; a simplification of Boyer and Moore 1977, 'A fast string searching algorithm', Commun. ACM 20(10). CLRS 4e ch. 32 (chapter only). Citations from memory; check before publishing.

The largest slide equals the pattern length (for a text letter not in the pattern), so a longer pattern allows longer jumps; on typical text Horspool reads about n/m letters, while its worst case is O(nm) (Horspool 1980; from memory).

claims.text: The text "HERE IS A SIMPLE EXAMPLE" has 24 characters, counting spaces.

recall.question: Searching right to left from a pattern's end, you meet a text letter that does not occur in the pattern at all. What can you do?
options: Slide the pattern past that letter entirely
Go back and re-read the text from the start
recall.why: No placement that covers a letter missing from the pattern can match, so the whole pattern jumps past it and those letters are never read.
